claim: Ramsey (1926) derived the probability laws from betting preferences and called them laws of consistency, not guides to truth; the Dutch book is a remark, and de Finetti (1937) and Kemeny/Lehman (1955) made it a finite theorem and converse.
agent_test: none: conceptual. Use only to justify the guardrail as consistency, not accuracy.

claim: The Dutch book theorem and converse hold only for finitely many bets; countable, diachronic and depragmatized versions need extra assumptions and are contested.
agent_test: none: scope limit on what the guardrail can claim.

claim: Coherence has an accuracy-dominance justification: for any incoherent credence set a coherent set is closer to the true values in every world, so forcing coherence cannot raise Brier loss. Dominance needs a continuous strictly proper score (SEP review); the original proofs were not opened.
agent_test: On a run set, check that Brier of renormalised answers is never worse than raw for the same samples.

claim: Human experts give incoherent probabilities over exclusive hypotheses: four-hypothesis sums average 1.54 to 1.77 (analysts) and 164% (medical prognoses), while binary complements sum near 1 (0.95-0.99).
agent_test: Elicit probabilities for 4 exclusive options with and without a forced-sum step; log the raw sum.

claim: Coherentizing analyst judgments cut error from MAE 0.23 to 0.15 (d=0.96, N=50), and averaging coherentized judgments reached 0.09.
agent_test: Raw vs normalised vs coherentized answer probabilities, equal tokens, exclusive-choice items, Brier.

claim: Simple normalisation (divide by the sum) did as well as or better than the fancier coherentization (MAE 0.13 vs 0.15), so a cheap rescale captures the gain.
agent_test: Compare plain normalisation against a coherence-projection step; expect no difference.

claim: Coherentizing is not magic: coherentized random responses gave MAE 0.21, so gains need signal in the raw judgments; ACH made raw sums worse (1.77 vs 1.54) yet accuracy after coherentizing was the same (diff 0.01).
agent_test: Run a structured-comparison operator and measure the raw sum before and after coherentising.

claim: Unpacking an event into parts raises its judged total (support theory): 31% vs 16% gastroenteritis; residual 50% on the short list vs 69% when unpacked.
agent_test: Ask for the residual 'other' option packed vs unpacked; check the sum.

claim: LLMs give incoherent probability judgments on identities like P(A)+P(not A)=1; larger models deviate less but none reach zero (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2 7B/70B, 24 event pairs).
agent_test: Ask for A and not-A separately and check |P+P-1|; compare with a forced-sum format at equal tokens.

claim: The Bayesian Sampler explains human incoherence better than the probability-theory-plus-noise model (67.8% of 59 in Exp 1; 61.9% of 84 in Exp 2), but several Exp 2 identity tests are null.
agent_test: Fit LLM identity deviations to the beta/(N+2beta) bias pattern to see if they are sampling bias.

claim: LLM forecasters violate consistency checks often: GPT-3.5 strong violations (>0.2) negation 52.6%, paraphrase 30.8%, Bayes rule 68.6%; GPT-4 10.9%, 12.5%, 58.8% (380 questions, 1220 variants).
agent_test: Re-ask each item in negated and paraphrased form; count strong violations for scaffold vs plain.

claim: Randomness does not explain the violations (under 20% of strong violations from resampling; 95% of answers identical over 5 passes), so resampling the same prompt does not cure incoherence.
agent_test: Compare spending tokens on resampling the same prompt vs on a consistency repair step.

claim: Prompting for consistency on one axis fixes that axis but can worsen others: GPT-4 negation violations 10.9% to 2.9% but paraphrase 12.5% to 17.3% and Bayes 58.8% to 68.6%.
agent_test: Add a consistency instruction and measure three check types, not only the targeted one.

claim: Consistency violations correlate with forecast error for some checks (Cond r=0.92 arbitrage, scraped set) but little or negatively for others (Negation -0.36, Or -0.24 on NewsAPI); the aggregate drops from 0.62-0.85 to 0.49-0.66 out of sample.
agent_test: Do not treat raw incoherence as a stand-in for accuracy on every check type; validate per check on our items.

claim: Training against arbitrage checks (ArbitrageForecaster, gpt-4o-mini, depth 0-4) lowers targeted violations but gives no reliable gain in ground-truth Brier or on untargeted checks.
agent_test: Prediction: forcing sum-to-one improves coherence while the accuracy gain stays small unless raw answers carry signal.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Arbitrage profit separates 15 LLMs far more than Brier: 0.002067 to 0.1994 (about 100x) vs Brier 0.1966 to 0.2157; Spearman 0.9143; 101 of 105 pairs distinguishable vs 32 for Brier.
agent_test: Use arbitrage profit as a cheap label-free monitor of the guardrail's effect on our agent.

claim: Irrelevant context raises LLM incoherence, up to an order of magnitude (anxiety, numeric anchor, coffee, savings exposure; instructions and headline arms), while a statistics arm and complement pairing reduce it.
agent_test: Add irrelevant context to the scaffold prompt and check raw-sum drift; keep complements together in elicitation.

claim: Richer logical structure exposes more incoherence: adding 16 joint cells raised mean arbitrage profit by 0.00244 (CI 0.001971-0.002961, 50 dates); a second stock in the prompt raised incoherence on the first.
agent_test: Elicit over a full partition and test joint vs marginal coherence.

claim: Incoherence persists in frontier models and ensembles: 4-LLM mid-tier panel residual > 0 on 33-94% of cliques; frontier panel 97.8% of 268 bets; showing the coupling in the prompt improved it (0.519 to 0.298, 16 of 20 partitions).
agent_test: Show all options of a partition in one prompt vs separate prompts.

claim: Across separate conversations models violate Bayesian-update axioms in over 50% of scenarios for nearly all model-constraint pairs; within one dialogue it falls to 10% for Gemini; non-reasoning updates cost over 30% of downstream success while reasoning models update near-exactly.
agent_test: Run update tasks with reasoning or code tool vs plain chain-of-thought at equal tokens.

claim: Bayes-consistency of belief updates improves only weakly with size (Llama 3 1.24B 0.658 to 8B 0.739), and batch updating usually beats sequential belief propagation.
agent_test: Batch the evidence into one update instead of updating sequentially.

claim: Verbal uncertainty words are closer to complementary in LLMs than in the human benchmark, with upward bias on negative words ('possible' 51 vs human 37).
agent_test: Use numeric rather than verbal probabilities when summing.

claim: Small models (1.5B-7B) had median cross-format incoherence below the pre-registered 0.05 threshold, yet 25% of propositions at 1.5B had book profit above 0.25; fine-tuning against exploitability cut negation exploitability about 100x but half the runs collapsed to an uninformative equilibrium.
agent_test: Warning: a coherence-only objective can be gamed; always pair it with an accuracy term.

claim: Coherence-based aggregation weights raised aggregate accuracy by more than 30% over the simple mean (second-hand figure).
agent_test: Weight multiple samples by their own sum-to-one deviation.

claim: Filtering for argumentative coherence raised GPT-4o accuracy 69% to 80% but discarded 1207 of 2923 questions, so part of the gain is selection.
agent_test: Compare with a matched random drop of the same size.

claim: Consistency-as-signal methods claim up to 4% accuracy gain on reasoning sets but a stress test reports paired p>=0.28 on four new domains.
agent_test: Treat consistency-as-signal gains as unproven until replicated on our own items.

claim: For multiple choice, the standard guardrail (softmax over option letters renormalised to 1) gives a confidence that ranks right above wrong answers (MSP AUROC beat chance in 245 of 280 cases across 15 chat LLMs; accuracy explains R2=0.94 of AUROC) but is not calibrated (accuracy explains R2=0.07 of calibration error).
agent_test: On a held-out set, compare AUROC and ECE of max renormalised option probability; set an abstain threshold from about 20 labelled items.

claim: Putting all exclusive options in one prompt and constraining mass to valid option tokens beats scoring options independently or leaving mass unconstrained: multiple-choice prompt beats cloze on 16 of 20 datasets (mean +9.7 points); prefilling raises first-token accuracy by +3.4 to +25.9 points and cuts ACE (Llama-3.1-8B MMLU 0.206 to 0.129). No study compares this at equal tokens to independent per-option probabilities with a sum check.
agent_test: Run the same items with (a) joint letter softmax with prefilled answer prefix, (b) independent per-option P(True) renormalised; compare accuracy and Brier at matched token cost.

claim: Renormalisation alone leaves systematic bias in which option gets the mass (position/ID prior: gold moved to D drops gpt-3.5-turbo MMLU 67.2 to 60.9; moved to A lifts llama-30b by 15.2). Prior correction (PriDe) or contextual calibration (up to +30.0 points on GPT-3) adds accuracy beyond plain renormalisation. A least-squares coherence projection for LLM samples is still untested.
agent_test: Shuffle option order and average the renormalised distributions; compare with single-order renormalisation.

claim: An explicit residual option does not reproduce human unpacking inflation in LLMs; instead models under-use 'none of the above' (52B model: accuracy and calibration of that option fall sharply on MMLU), so named options absorb residual mass. The guardrail must force residual mass explicitly.
agent_test: Add an 'other' option with explicit instruction and check whether named-option sum falls toward 1 minus the base rate of other.

claim: Asking for top-k guesses with probabilities in one response lowers ECE on hard sets (ChatGPT TruthfulQA 0.389, 0.361, 0.203 for k=1,2,4) and was best for GPT-3.5 in a broader benchmark, but no single prompt wins and discrimination (AUROC) stays weak.
agent_test: Compare k=1 vs k=4 elicitation ECE on a held-out set.

claim: Which Dutch book version justifies the guardrail for a non-betting agent: pragmatic versions need bets accepted; depragmatized versions still rely on value judgements; the accuracy-dominance theorem (strictly proper score, e.g. 0.6/0.6 on X and not-X is dominated by 0.5/0.5 with Brier 0.52 vs 0.50 in every world) needs no bettor but holds only for strictly proper scores. Design consequence: justify the guardrail by Brier-type accuracy, and use diachronic books only to motivate pre-committed update rules.
agent_test: none: conceptual.
